title: Working out tax on shares
body:
O.P.
I'm investing full-time in shares, and curious to find out if my accountant is doing my tax correctly. Rather than adding up all the profits and losses from shares sold during the financial year, he's subtracting the 'Purchases' from 'Sales' (on my CMC trading account) and saying that's my 'Net Business Income'. That looks strange to me since most of those 'Purchases' are shares I haven't sold yet, so does that sound correct please?

---- replies ----
[User #18356030285 postspgdownloadWhirlpool Forums Addict] Sounds a bit dodgy. Appears he's classifying you as a professional share trader (usually day traders etc.) rather than as an individual that buys and sells shares infrequently. They get treated differently for tax purposes.
Yes, the unsold shares must be accounted for (perhaps you missed where they did that)
AI: If you don't add back the value of the unsold shares as Closing Stock at the end of the financial year, the calculation will incorrectly depress your taxable income (or show a massive, incorrect loss). Maybe the accountant wants to pretend they're saving you lots of money?
Note a big drawback as a share trader is you don't get the 50% CGT discount. That may be less important for shares you buy now but your existing (grandfathered) shares will probably benefit a lot from that if you sell after 12 months of owning them.
I'd be asking the accountant:
1) Why he's classifying you as a Share Trader and not a Share Investor and 2) Are they adding the value of your unsold shares (as of June 30) back into the equation?
NB I am not an accountant.

I'm investing Understand the difference between investing & trading. A lot of people who say they’re “investing” are really trading or gambling. Read Buffett.

https://www.ato.gov.au/indiv iduals-and-families/investme nts-and-assets/capital-gains -tax/shares-and-similar-inve stments/share-investing-versus-share-trading

[User #79475887 postsgoblin1Participant] O.P.
Thanks for your responses! Yes bm123 I got advice on a somewhat different situation two years ago, where my agent was still treating me as a share trader. Since then he agreed I was an investor (almost all my trades are held for over a year) and I've been treated as an investor and allowed to get the 50% CGT discount. However based on what people are saying here, it sounds like my accountant might be treating my situation incorrectly. My main complaint is that, based on my buys and sells, I only made a profit of about $30k last year. However my accountant, subtracting the 'Purchases' from 'Sales' (based on data from my CMC trading account) informs me that I made a profit of about $110k – a huge difference, and based on mostly purchases that I haven't sold yet. So my question now would be, does it sound like my accountant is doing this correctly or not?
[User #18356030285 postspgdownloadWhirlpool Forums Addict] goblin1 writes...
I made a profit of about $110k
Is "profit" the right word? You can't just subtract 'Purchases' from 'Sales' (read my post again). You need to add back in your current holdings, which sounds like that's what the $80K difference is?
[User #79475887 postsgoblin1Participant] O.P.
Subtracting Purchases from Sales is basically what he's done (actually coming up with a net profit of $105k, not $110k as I thought):
From my CMC cash transaction summary: Sales 451,798.63 Purchases 340,214.22
Email from my accountant:
"Regarding the net business income of $105,123, this relates to your share trading activity through CMC Invest. As per the CMC report and your own summary:
Total income: $451,798.63 Total purchases: $340,214.22
We have also allowed for:
Depreciation: $323 Other expenses (CMC fees, home office, internet, stationery, subscriptions, and accounting fees): $6,139
This results in the net profit of $105,123."
[User #79475887 postsgoblin1Participant] O.P.
So I guess I should be asking: is the above method the one generally used for share traders (rather than investors) at tax time?

Read this information from ATO

My accountant agreed with me two years ago that I'm an investor – that's why I'm now getting the CGT discount on my holdings. It would appear now however that he's still using the method applied to traders to work out my taxable income (as far as I can gather.)

goblin1 writes...
I'm an investor Just because he agreed with you does not make it right. Did you actually read the ATO information, in particular this. Make absolutely sure. I am not telling you whether it's right or wrong, just to cross all your Ts and dot all your Is. "Repetition, volume and regularity
Repetition is the frequency of transactions or the number of similar transactions. It is a key characteristic of business activities.
The higher the volume of your share transactions, the more likely it is that you are carrying on a business.
A business of share trading would also be expected to involve the purchase of shares on a regular basis through a regular or routine method"
Else writes...
profit and loss statement Also, an individual is unlikely to have one of these, traditionally they are prepared for businesses.
[User #7964355157 postsbm123Whirlpool Forums Addict] goblin1 writes...
My accountant agreed with me two years ago that I'm an investor – that's why I'm now getting the CGT discount on my holdings. It would appear now however that he's still using the method applied to traders to work out my taxable income (as far as I can gather.)
How were your last 2 (or more) tax returns completed, in the same way as this?
If so it sounds like it is being done as a trader, not investor. If you haven’t had a change in trading patterns then it may be hard to argue why you’re now wanting to change to be treated as an investor (getting a CGT discount is not a valid reason)..
I think you need to seek out better professional advice.
[User #56703218982 postsArrowmanWhirlpool Forums Addict] @goblin1 This looks very odd. Either your accountant is utterly incompetent, or you are misunderstanding something.
goblin1 writes...
Yes bm123 I got advice on a somewhat different situation two years ago, where my agent was still treating me as a share trader. Since then he agreed I was an investor (almost all my trades are held for over a year) and I've been treated as an investor and allowed to get the 50% CGT discount.
So you've done (your accountant has done) at least one full year's tax return since then? And that tax return includes capital gains using the 50% discount, and no "share trading" activity or claims for expenses?
However based on what people are saying here, it sounds like my accountant might be treating my situation incorrectly. My main complaint is that, based on my buys and sells, I only made a profit of about $30k last year.
To be clear: Your "profit" or gain from shares during the year (that contributes to your taxable income) is based only on sells (and the difference between the sell price and the buy price, possibly discounted by 50%). Your "buys" are completely irrelevant; they are only relevant if you are operating as a trader (or for recording the cost base against which a future sell can be measured).
goblin1 writes...
Email from my accountant:
"Regarding the net business income of $105,123, this relates to your share trading activity through CMC Invest. As per the CMC report and your own summary:
Total income: $451,798.63 Total purchases: $340,214.22
We have also allowed for:
Depreciation: $323 Other expenses (CMC fees, home office, internet, stationery, subscriptions, and accounting fees): $6,139
This results in the net profit of $105,123."
If you are actually operating as an investor, that email makes no sense at all. As an investor you do not calculate a "net profit" by measuring sales (income) vs purchases, and you do not get to claim expenses.
Something is very "off" here. I suggest you need to ask your accountant:
Why are you calculating a "net profit" and why are you including expenses, when I am operating as an investor, not a trader? Why are you referring to "net business income" which is something only relevant to a trader?
And most importantly – Are you going to be including net business income of $105,123 in my tax return (because that would be a gross overstatement of taxable income)?
As I said before – from what you are saying, either your accountant is grossly incompetent and you need to run far away from them, or there is a fundamental misunderstanding on your part about what is going on.
[User #7964355157 postsbm123Whirlpool Forums Addict] goblin1 writes...
I'm investing full-time in shares
Do you mean your only source of income is through share ‘investing’?
It does sound like you are operating as a share trader.
EDIT: Your thread from 2 years ago is really the same general question. Your statement then answers the question, you have put ‘Share trader’ as your occupation on your tax return ‘for some years’…
goblin1 writes...
my agent has been putting as my occupation for some years. The actual wording of my agent in the email was "Since you are in the business of trading stocks, you are not eligible for the 50% CGT discount."
[User #56703218982 postsArrowmanWhirlpool Forums Addict] bm123 writes...
Do you mean your only source of income is through share ‘investing’?
It does sound like you are operating as a share trader.
Not necessarily. You can choose to operate as a trader, by meeting the ATO criteria, but you don't HAVE to operate as a trader – this is a status you ask/apply for, not something the ATO imposes on you unilaterally.
A retired person can happily continue to operate their share portfolio as an investor, even if it is their only source of income.
At least that is what I have taken from the various googles I have done on this subject, including the ATO's own website, and I haven't seen anyone contradict it on whirlpool.
